newsitem.title: FRANCE: African protesters re-occupy Paris church.
newsitem.headline: African protesters re-occupy Paris church.

text.p: About 30 Africans evicted from a Paris church two months ago briefly occupied the building again on Sunday, saying tough French immigration laws were keeping them in a legal twilight.
"We can't allow our problem to drag on and on...the government has to open talks," said Doro Traore, a spokesman for the Africans after the new sit-in at the Saint-Bernard church.

A few dozen riot police, who used axes to smash their way into the church two months ago to evict about 210 Africans including 10 men on a 50-day hunger strike, ringed the church after the Africans stayed on after a morning Mass.

There were no arrests as the Africans left in late afternoon, surrounded by well-wishers. The Africans went to church partly to mourn one of the hunger strikers, 35-year-old Malian Amaro Fofana, who died of cancer on Wednesday.

"We're not terrorists, we're not living secretly in France but we simply lack the legal documents to stay," said Aboubakar Diop, a spokesman for the group. "We're asking (the authorities) to legalise us."

"We came here to pray, then they surrounded the church. They're responsible for what's happening," he said of the riot police. Others among the Africans, however, said they decided on the symbolic occupation last Thursday.
And the Saint-Bernard priest said "we left as friends but we weren't happy about this way of occupying the site without warning."

Traore said seven of the original group of Africans were in jail, 13 had been expelled and 88 had been granted residence papers. Most of the rest, many of them from Mali, Senegal or Zaire, were still uncertain if they could stay or not.
"It's completely arbitrary. There are no objective criteria," he said. "Tomorrow or the next day maybe we'll occupy a new place."
The Africans originally occupied the Saint-Bernard church to protest at 1993 reforms that outlawed some immigrants who were previously legally in France.

Diop accused the government of going back on promises that it would not separate families and that it would not expel sick people. "They have expelled sick people, heads of familes...they've lied throughout," he said.
The Africans said Fofana's death was partly related to his his fast, even though doctors say his illness was fatal.

"People who are not legally in France are scared of going to hospital out of fear of being denounced to the police," said Madjiguene Cisse, a spokeswoman for the Africans. The Africans planned rallies in coming days for Fofana.
